newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African rand seen ending 1997 at 4.70/dlr -fund.
newsitem.headline: S.African rand seen ending 1997 at 4.70/dlr -fund.

text.p: South Africa's rand is seen ending the year at around 4.70 on the U.S. dollar, depreciating substantially less than inflation differentials, according to Sandra Gordon, economist at fund manager Syfrets.
Gordon said an anticipated easing in balance of payments pressures which would help to rebuild reserves would stabilise the rand in 1997 after its sharp 29 percent slide against the dollar last year.

This scenario, together with an expected slowdown in credit demand and a peak in inflation in April, pointed to an anticipated one percentage point cut in interest rates around mid-year and a second cut towards year-end, she said.
Gordon, however, cautioned that the rand may experience a period of renewed weakness in the early months of 1997 before stabilising later.

"(There) could be a mismatch between the inflow of privatisation proceeds (likely to begin during the second quarter at the earliest) and the fact that the bulk of this year's capital payments fall due during the first quarter."
Current dollar strength against other major currencies may also weaken the rand, she said in a a report.
Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals told Reuters last week he saw scope for a very stable rand this year, buoyed by a sharply better balance of payments position.
The rand has made strong gains since the beginning of the January when it was hovering above the 4.70 level to trade as low as 4.5580 bid on the dollar on Friday.

Gordon said a marked slowdown in local demand for imports, coupled with improved export earnings, was expected to ensure a narrowing of the current account deficit. The current account was estimated to have registered a small surplus in the fourth quarter of 1996.
"After registering a current account deficit of close to 10 billion rand last year, a marked narrowing to around three billion is anticipated in 1997," she said.

Foreign capital inflows were also expected to resume this year, despite some scheduled debt repayment, as government's privatisation programme with its emphasis on foreign strategic partners gathered steam.

Together a narrowing current account deficit and net inflow of foreign capital would help to rebuild gold and foreign exchange reserves, underpinning the rand and easing upward pressure on short-term interest rates, she said.

"A rebuilding of the reserves, coupled with a period of renewed stability in the rand, would do much to bolster foreign sentiment towards South Africa...(and) encourage foreign investors to increase their exposure to local financial markets."
Gordon said a high interest rate environment should ensure a slowdown in domestic demand this year as credit extension, which funded a large portion of a recent consumer spending boom, had peaked.
However, consumer inflation was expected to trend marginally higher during the months ahead, peaking at marginally below 10 percent in April before declining once more.
"A level of 7.5 percent is anticipated by year-end. An average inflation rate of 8.8 percent is anticipated in 1997," she said.

Gordon said South Africa's export earnings should be boosted significantly this year amid a still weak rand coupled with an inticipated increase in dollar commodity prices as world economies experieced a modest rebound.

"Furthermore, South Africa's export volumes are expected to benefit from the anticipated recovery in global economies, notably our major Euopean trading partners, and from continued strong growth in world trade," Gordon said.
